intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you something to remember or warns where people slip. Work the examples in pencil, answer the recall questions before you check, and add your own marks beside mine.

sections.title: Why the early grades decide later learning
sections.big_idea: Grade 3 is the turning point from learning to read to **reading to learn**, and children who miss it fall further behind every year.
in_plain_words: FLN is the set of skills a child needs before school subjects can be learned at all: reading a simple text with understanding, writing words and short sentences, and handling numbers and the four operations. Every later subject assumes a child can read the textbook and handle its numbers. NIPUN Bharat uses Grade 3 as the inflection point.

Curricula keep moving whether or not children keep up, so learning profiles are shallow. In Delhi, the average grade 6 student was 2.5 grade levels behind, and one classroom spanned five or six levels. **Slowing down to match children** is what Pritchett and Beatty argue raises learning. Learning poverty puts the scale in view: 70% of 10-year-olds in low- and middle-income countries after the pandemic.

worked_example.title: Where is the average child?
worked_example.setup: Muralidharan, Singh and Ganimian found the average grade 6 student 2.5 grade levels below standard in maths, and 4.5 levels behind by grade 9.
steps: A grade 6 student works at grade 6 − 2.5 = 3.5 in maths.
A grade 9 student works at grade 9 − 4.5 = 4.5 in maths.
The deficit grew from 2.5 to 4.5 levels: 4.5 − 2.5 = 2 more levels behind.
So each year of schooling added less than a year of learning.
worked_example.answer: The average grade 6 child works near level 3.5, and the average grade 9 child near level 4.5. The gap grows with schooling.

mistakes: Treating FLN as a Grade 1 problem. The deficit grows through grade 9 if nobody addresses it.
Quoting 70% learning poverty as a measured figure. The World Bank calls it an estimate simulated from school closure data.
Teaching to the textbook in a class with a five or six level spread. It reaches only the top of the range.

recall.q: What phrase does NIPUN Bharat use for Grade 3?
recall.a: The inflection point by which children "learn to read" so they can "read to learn".

recall.q: What is a learning profile?
recall.a: The relationship between years of schooling and the skills a child has.

recall.q: How many grade levels does one grade span, per Muralidharan, Singh and Ganimian?
recall.a: Five to six.

recall.q: What does learning poverty measure?
recall.a: The share of children of late primary age (about 10) who cannot read and understand a simple text, counting out-of-school children as not reading.

recall.q: In which countries did RISE run its country research?
recall.a: Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Nigeria, Pakistan, Tanzania and Vietnam.

sections.title: How children learn to read
sections.big_idea: Reading is a **ladder of five components**, and diagnosis means finding the earliest rung where the child is stuck.
in_plain_words: The EGRA Toolkit names five components: phonological awareness, phonics, vocabulary, fluency and comprehension. Comprehension is the goal and the others are the route. Reading rests on oral language, so a child who cannot answer questions about a story she hears has a language problem that phonics will not fix.

Decoding turns symbols into words, and invented words test it because memory cannot help. Fluency frees attention for meaning, and NIPUN Bharat sets 45 to 60 words a minute in Grade 2 and at least 60 in Grade 3, always with meaning. Writing grows beside reading. **Dictation shows what a child knows**, where copying shows only eye and hand.

key_terms.meaning: Noticing and working with the sound units of spoken language.
Working out written words from the link between symbols and sounds.
Invented words that force a child to decode.
Words read correctly per minute.
A question whose answer is in the text.
A question needing the text plus the child's reasoning.

worked_example.title: Place four children on the pathway
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a teacher meets four Grade 3 children and uses the pathway table.
steps: Asha cannot name most aksharas, so she is at symbol knowledge and needs daily symbol-sound practice.
Bilal knows aksharas but cannot read words, so he needs blending and decoding.
Chitra reads words but stumbles on sentences, so she needs repeated reading of short, easy texts.
Dev reads fluently but cannot answer questions, so check language and comprehension with talk and questioning.
worked_example.answer: Symbol practice for Asha, decoding for Bilal, fluency for Chitra, language and comprehension for Dev.

mistakes: Adding more phonics for a child who cannot answer questions when listening. The problem is language.
Reporting speed alone. Children can be drilled to bark at print, so report fluency with comprehension.
Treating copying from the board as writing. Dictation shows what the child knows.

recall.q: Name the five components of reading.
recall.a: Phonological awareness, phonics, vocabulary, fluency and comprehension.

recall.q: Why does EGRA use nonwords?
recall.a: So the child cannot rely on memory and must decode.

recall.q: What are NIPUN Bharat's fluency goals?
recall.a: 45 to 60 words per minute in Grade 2, and at least 60 in Grade 3, read with meaning.

recall.q: How does the deck suggest testing oral language?
recall.a: Read a short story aloud and ask questions.

recall.q: Why must benchmarks be set per language?
recall.a: Languages differ in word length and scripts differ in visual density.

sections.title: Scripts of South Asia: alphabets and aksharas
sections.big_idea: Most South Asian children read in an **akshara script**, which takes longer to master than an alphabet, so timelines copied from English will fail.
in_plain_words: Scripts fall into three kinds. An alphabet writes a single sound, an abjad mainly consonants, and an alphasyllabary writes a consonant with an inherent vowel changed by signs and joined into conjuncts. Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu and Kannada are alphasyllabaries. In क the vowel is inherent, and in कि the vowel sign is written before but read after.

Nag's studies of Kannada found that akshara knowledge comes more slowly than letter knowledge in English, even in effective schools, and that phoneme awareness grows with print. Symbol learning continues into middle school. **Teach the vowel signs as a pattern**, begin with syllables, add frequent conjuncts early, and keep teaching symbols through Grade 3.

key_terms.meaning: The written unit of an alphasyllabary.
A vowel sign attached to a consonant.
Two or more consonants fused into one symbol.
Rapid automatised naming: how fast a child names familiar items.
The chart of a consonant combined with each vowel sign.

worked_example.title: Read the akshara table
worked_example.setup: A child meets क, का, कि, कु and क्ष on a card.
steps: क is a consonant with the inherent vowel, read ka.
का has a vowel sign after the consonant, read kaa.
कि has a vowel sign written before but read after, read ki.
कु has a sign below, read ku, and क्ष is a conjunct of k and sha, read ksha.
worked_example.answer: ka, kaa, ki, ku, ksha. Three position patterns for vowel signs plus one conjunct, all from one consonant.

mistakes: Copying a letter-a-week English schedule. Hindi or Telugu then leaves most vowel sign combinations and conjuncts untaught.
Chanting the barakhadi daily without reading. It trains recitation.
Starting with phoneme games. Syllable-level games come first in akshara readers.

recall.q: What does an alphasyllabary symbol stand for?
recall.a: A consonant with an inherent vowel, changed by vowel signs and joined into conjuncts.

recall.q: What did Nag (2007) find about akshara knowledge?
recall.a: It takes longer to acquire than letter knowledge in English, across grades and in both low-achieving and effective schools.

recall.q: Which predicts reading rate besides orthographic knowledge and phoneme awareness?
recall.a: Rapid automatised naming.

recall.q: Which NEP paragraph sets the order of languages?
recall.a: Para 4.12: early reading and writing in the mother tongue, other languages from Grade 3 and beyond.

recall.q: What does Nag mean by alphabetism?
recall.a: Treating the alphabet as the model of how all reading works.

sections.title: Early number sense
sections.big_idea: Number sense and place value come **before written procedures**, and children bring arithmetic from the market that school can build on.
in_plain_words: Foundational numeracy covers pre-number concepts, numbers and operations, shapes, measurement, data and patterns, so a sums-only programme leaves most of it out. Number sense means counting with one-to-one correspondence, knowing the last count is the total, and placing numbers on a line. Siegler and Ramani found a numbered board game closed the gap for low-income preschoolers.

Place value is where many stall: ASER 2024 shows 33.7% of Std III children can subtract with borrowing. Teach it as concrete, pictorial, symbolic, then talk and apply. Banerjee, Duflo and colleagues found that **market children calculate well at work** but not in school format, and school children the reverse, so connect the two explicitly.

diagram.caption: keep the symbol attached to its meaning

key_terms.meaning: Intuitive grasp of quantity, order and how to split it.
The last count word tells the total.
The 4 in 43 means four tens.
Opening a ten to subtract.
NIPUN Bharat learning goal for a year.

worked_example.title: Subtract 43 − 17 with sticks
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a Grade 2 class uses 4 bundles of ten and 3 loose sticks.
steps: Show 43 as 4 tens and 3 ones. Taking away 7 ones needs more ones than 3.
Open one ten: 3 tens and 13 ones.
Take 7 from 13 ones: 13 − 7 = 6.
Take 1 ten from 3 tens: 3 − 1 = 2, leaving 2 tens and 6 ones.
worked_example.answer: 43 − 17 = 26. Only after this should children write the borrowing procedure.

mistakes: Teaching written sums before a child can compare quantities. She may get 4 + 3 right and not know whether 7 sweets are more than 5.
Skipping the talk step. Children should explain why a ten was opened.
Ignoring market arithmetic. Start from money, measures and trade.

recall.q: Name the six components of NIPUN Bharat's numeracy list.
recall.a: Pre-number concepts, numbers and operations, shapes and spatial understanding, measurement, data handling, patterns.

recall.q: What did the numbered board game study find?
recall.a: Four 15-minute sessions closed the gap in numerical estimation, and the colour version had no effect.

recall.q: What share of Std III rural children could subtract in 2024?
What did Banerjee, Duflo and colleagues find in Kolkata and Delhi markets?
recall.a: Working children used complex arithmetic at work yet could not solve equal abstract problems; school children showed the reverse.

recall.q: What is the Grade 2 numeracy lakshya in the 2021 document?
recall.a: Reads and writes numbers up to 999 and subtracts numbers up to 99.

sections.title: Measuring foundational learning
sections.big_idea: Oral, one-on-one tools show **where a child is**, and each tool answers one question, so quote every figure with its method and year.
in_plain_words: A written test is a reading test for a child who cannot read. So ASER, EGRA, EGMA and the FLS sit an assessor with one child. ASER is a household survey of rural India, run the same way since 2006, with reading and arithmetic ladders. In 2024 it reached 6,49,491 children, and reading in government schools recovered past 2018.

The same story needs care. PARAKH tests children in school on written items and reports an average, while ASER reports the share reaching a level, so a 64% average and a 23% reading rate (ASER, government school Std III) can both be true. States differ by a factor of seven. **Match the tool to the decision**, and never use a sample survey to judge a teacher.

key_terms.meaning: Household survey of rural learning, run with Pratham.
Oral early grade reading and mathematics toolkits from RTI.
The Foundational Learning Study of Grade 3, in 20 languages.
National Assessment Centre set up in NCERT in 2023.
A ladder from letters upward that shows where a child is.

worked_example.title: Read the ASER 2024 changes
worked_example.setup: Rural India, Std III subtraction (all schools): 28.2% in 2018 and 33.7% in 2024. Std VIII division: 44.1% in 2018 and 45.8% in 2024.
steps: Std III gain since 2018: 33.7 − 28.2 = 5.5 percentage points.
Std VIII gain since 2018: 45.8 − 44.1 = 1.7 percentage points.
Std VIII children who could not divide in 2024: 100 − 45.8 = 54.2%.
FLS 2022 numeracy: 42 + 10 = 52% met or exceeded global minimum proficiency.
worked_example.answer: Std III gained 5.5 points and Std VIII 1.7, and 54.2% of Std VIII children could not divide. The upper grades have barely moved.

mistakes: Comparing an ASER share with a PARAKH average. Samples, tests and metrics differ.
Using EGRA for high-stakes judgements of teachers. The Toolkit says it is not intended for that.
Comparing languages in FLS as if only script differed. Each language sample is also a state school system.

recall.q: Why test one child at a time orally?
recall.a: A written test tells only what children do not know, and an oral test shows where they are in learning to read.

recall.q: What are ASER's reading and arithmetic ladders?
recall.a: Reading: letters, words, Std I paragraph, Std II story. Arithmetic: numbers 1 to 9, 11 to 99, subtraction, division.

recall.q: How many Grade 3 children did FLS 2022 assess?
recall.a: More than 86,000 in about 10,000 schools.

recall.q: What share of rural Std III children could read a Std II text in 2024?
recall.a: 27.1% across all schools.

recall.q: When did PARAKH begin and when was its first survey?
recall.a: Set up 8 February 2023; first survey tested on 4 December 2024.

sections.title: Indian policy: NEP 2020, NIPUN Bharat and the RTE Act
sections.big_idea: NEP 2020 made FLN **the first priority**, NIPUN Bharat turned it into a mission, and the RTE Act supplies the legal hooks.
in_plain_words: NEP 2020 chapter 2 says the highest priority is universal FLN in primary school by 2025, and sets the 5+3+3+4 structure with a foundational stage for ages 3 to 8. NIPUN Bharat launched on 5 July 2021 and moved the target year to 2026-27. Ministry replies since December 2025 describe the goal as the end of Grade 2, with no year. The curriculum framework (NCF-FS) and the Jadui Pitara kit followed.

The RTE Act does not use the phrase foundational literacy, but section 29(2)(e), (f) and (h) and section 24(1)(d) speak to activity-based teaching, mother tongue, continuous evaluation and a duty to assess each child. **Section 16 was rewritten in 2019** to allow exams in Classes 5 and 8 with extra instruction. ASER 2024 shows real progress, though about one in four Std III children reads a Std II text.

events.what: RTE Act gives content to Art. 21A

diagram.caption: from the Act to the mission

key_terms.meaning: NEP structure covering ages 3 to 18.
Three years pre-school plus Grades 1 and 2, ages 3 to 8.
Twelve-week play-based module at the start of Grade 1.
Play-based kit based on NCF-FS.
Additional instruction and re-exam within two months.

worked_example.title: Use the RTE hooks
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an NGO wants the legal basis for three practices in its programme.
steps: Activity-based pedagogy: section 29(2)(e), learning through activities, discovery and exploration.
Teaching in the mother tongue: section 29(2)(f), as far as practicable.
Diagnosing each child: section 24(1)(d), teachers assess learning ability and supplement instruction.
Catch-up for late entrants: the proviso to section 4, a right to special training.
worked_example.answer: Section 29(2)(e), 29(2)(f), 24(1)(d) and the proviso to section 4. Cite the section when you argue for the practice.

mistakes: Treating NEP as enforceable. The policy has no statutory force.
Quoting one target year for NIPUN Bharat. It moved from 2025 to 2026-27, and later replies give no year.
Reporting that a readiness programme ran as proof that children are ready.

recall.q: What does NEP 2020 para 2.2 set as the highest priority?
recall.a: Universal foundational literacy and numeracy in primary school by 2025.

recall.q: What ages does the Foundational Stage cover?
recall.a: 3 to 8, with three years of pre-school plus Grades 1 and 2.

recall.q: When was NIPUN Bharat launched, and under which scheme?
recall.a: 5 July 2021, under Samagra Shiksha.

recall.q: What does RTE s 24(1)(d) require of teachers?
recall.a: To assess the learning ability of each child and supplement additional instruction as required.

recall.q: How far did Himachal Pradesh's Std III reading rise from 2022 to 2024?
recall.a: From 23.0% to 49.7%, about 27 points.

sections.title: Programmes and evidence
sections.big_idea: The strongest evidence favours **teaching at the right level and structured pedagogy**, while inputs alone fail.
in_plain_words: GEEAP's 2023 update names Great Buys that include targeting instruction by learning level and structured pedagogy. TaRL regroups children by what they can do, using a simple oral test and a fixed daily period. The balsakhi study found 0.28 SD gains and the Jaunpur reading camps raised reading, while information alone changed nothing.

Scaling in government is where methods break. Bihar and Uttarakhand teachers did not adopt TaRL, Haryana gained 0.15 SD and Uttar Pradesh camps gained 0.61 to 0.70 SD. Mindspark software raised maths by 0.37 SD. **Inputs without routines fail**, so tie every book and kit to a daily period and a check on use.

key_terms.meaning: Global panel rating cost-effective education approaches.
Teaching at the Right Level: grouping children by skill across grades.
Lesson plans, materials and ongoing teacher support together.
Standard deviation, the unit for effect sizes.
Adaptive software serving content at the child's level.

worked_example.title: Compare two TaRL trials
worked_example.setup: Haryana: a dedicated hour of level-based teaching gave a language gain of 0.15 SD. Uttar Pradesh: 40-day camps run by Pratham volunteers gave 0.61 to 0.70 SD.
steps: Take the lower UP figure: 0.61 ÷ 0.15 = 4.07.
So the camp gain is about four times the teacher-led hour.
The camps ran during school hours with Pratham volunteers, so they were intensive.
Use 0.15 SD as the cautious benchmark for a government teacher-led hour.
worked_example.answer: The UP camps gained about four times as much as Haryana's hour. Use Haryana's 0.15 SD as the sober planning benchmark.

mistakes: Treating laptops or readers as a programme. Hardware or inputs alone are rated Bad Buys.
Assuming a volunteer model transfers to government teachers. Bihar and Uttarakhand teachers did not adopt it.
Reading one study as settled. Mindspark's gains were measured after-school, with a limited evidence base at scale.

recall.q: Name two GEEAP Great Buys.
recall.a: Structured pedagogy, and targeting teaching by learning level.

recall.q: What were the five TaRL steps?
recall.a: Assess, group, teach, reassess, return.

recall.q: What did the Jaunpur reading camps achieve?
recall.a: A child who could read nothing was 60 percentage points more likely to decipher letters a year later.

recall.q: What did Mindspark lottery winners gain after 4.5 months?
recall.a: 0.37 SD in maths and 0.23 SD in Hindi.

recall.q: What was the size of Nepal's early grade reading programme?
recall.a: A five-year, USD 71 million programme in all 77 districts.

sections.title: Mother tongue and multilingual classrooms
sections.big_idea: The law backs mother tongue teaching with **different force from each source**, and private schools may choose the medium.
in_plain_words: Many children start school in a language they do not speak at home. NEP 2020 para 4.11 says the medium until at least Grade 5 will be the home language wherever possible. Article 350A is an obligation of endeavour, RTE s 29(2)(f) says as far as practicable, and the 2014 Constitution Bench judgment in Associated Management struck down compulsory mother tongue for unaided and minority schools.

Rooms with four or five home languages need a multilingual approach, because teaching each child in her own language is impossible, and tribal-language programmes such as Odisha's show better engagement but thin evidence. FLS 2022 found the share unable to do basic tasks ranging from 7% in Punjabi to 42% in Tamil. **Always state the language of assessment** beside a reading figure.

key_terms.meaning: Mother tongue based multilingual education.
Endeavour to teach linguistic minorities in the mother tongue.
The language in which lessons are taught.
A check that separates language from decoding.
Teaching with two languages, including bilingual materials.

worked_example.title: Choose the first reading language
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a team applies the decision table to three situations in a government school system.
steps: Home language is the state language: first reading language is the state language, with oral English early and reading English from Grade 3.
Home language is a distinct tribal language with a script and materials: use the home language and bridge to the state language by Grade 3.
Home language has no materials: use the state language with bilingual support and local assistants.
FLS spread check: 42 − 7 = 35 percentage points between Tamil and Punjabi on basic tasks.
worked_example.answer: State language, home language with a bridge, state language with bilingual support. The 35-point FLS spread shows one benchmark cannot suit all languages.

mistakes: Citing NEP para 4.11 as binding. It is policy and not enforceable in court.
Assuming the State can compel mother tongue medium in private unaided or minority schools. The 2014 judgment says it cannot.
Treating English medium demand as irrelevant. Parental demand is a fact any programme must work with.

recall.q: What does NEP 2020 say about the medium of instruction?
recall.a: Wherever possible, at least until Grade 5 and preferably Grade 8 and beyond, the home language, mother tongue, local or regional language.

recall.q: What did the Supreme Court decide on 6 May 2014?
recall.a: The State cannot compel the mother tongue as medium in unaided and minority schools.

recall.q: How does the deck define mother tongue under Article 350A?
recall.a: The language of the linguistic minority group the child belongs to, as decided by the parent or guardian.

recall.q: Which states appear in the tribal-language review?
recall.a: Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.

recall.q: How can you separate a language problem from a decoding problem?
recall.a: Ask the child to listen to a story and answer questions, as EGRA's listening comprehension subtask does.

sections.title: Teachers, materials, coaching and families
sections.big_idea: FLN depends on **teachers who practise, coaches who visit and time that is protected**, and inputs alone rarely change learning.
in_plain_words: NIPUN Bharat trains the existing workforce through NISHTHA. Coaching raised teachers' practice by 0.49 SD and student achievement by 0.18 SD, though effects shrink at scale: a coach with 60 schools becomes an inspector. Training with larger gains links participation to career incentives and has teachers practise in the session. Government programmes at scale usually lack these features.

Small schools are the norm: 52.1% of government primary schools had fewer than 60 students, and two-thirds of Std I and II classrooms were multigrade. Materials must be graded readers children can read, and time must be protected. Families help in small ways, and communities do better with specific tasks. **Child data needs consent**: DPDP s 9 applies from 13 May 2027.

diagram.caption: six things a programme must deliver together

key_terms.meaning: NCERT's integrated in-service teacher training.
An expert observes, gives feedback and models, repeatedly.
One teacher teaching more than one grade.
Short books ordered by difficulty.
Parental consent required for a child's data under s 9.

worked_example.title: Read the attendance and school-size figures
worked_example.setup: ASER 2024: student attendance 75.9%; small government primary schools 52.1% in 2024 and 44% in 2022.
steps: Share of students absent on the visit day: 100 − 75.9 = 24.1%.
Rise in small schools since 2022: 52.1 − 44 = 8.1 percentage points.
Small schools need two teachers by law for up to 60 children.
So multigrade teaching is the typical case, and grouping across grades suits it.
worked_example.answer: About 24.1% of students were absent, and small schools rose by 8.1 points. Design for multigrade rooms from the start.

mistakes: Assuming a coaching pilot's effect holds at scale. Larger trials show smaller effects.
Writing lesson scripts for one grade. Two-thirds of Std I and II classrooms are multigrade.
Giving communities information and expecting change. In Jaunpur it did nothing.

recall.q: What did Kraft, Blazar and Hogan find for coaching?
recall.a: 0.49 SD on teachers' practice and 0.18 SD on student achievement, from 60 studies.

recall.q: What three questions make a training checklist?
recall.a: Is it subject-specific, do teachers practise in the session, and who visits the classroom afterwards?

recall.q: What share of government primary schools used books other than textbooks in 2024?
What does RTE s 27 allow as non-teaching duties?
recall.a: Only the decennial census, disaster relief and elections.

recall.q: What did the maternal literacy study find?
recall.a: All three interventions had significant but modest impacts on children's maths scores.

sections.title: A practitioner's toolkit
sections.big_idea: Test every child with a five-minute card, **group by level**, reassess every few weeks, and check the plan before scaling.
in_plain_words: The diagnostic uses the ASER logic: one card in the school language, one child at a time, five steps from aksharas to comprehension and a word problem. The results sort a class into groups, and the teacher reassesses every three weeks so a child moves when she reaches the next level. The aim is that Group A is empty by term end.

Planning a block adds diagnosis, design, support, materials and review. The decision table links situations to the option with the strongest evidence, and costing divides the total by children reached. **A yes to every scaling question is no guarantee**, but any no is a known reason for failure, so run the ten-question checklist first.

diagram.caption: the loop that moves children up

key_terms.meaning: A five-step card placing a child on a ladder.
Children needing sounds, symbols and blending.
Maps a field situation to the strongest option.
Total cost divided by children reached.
Ten questions to answer before expanding a pilot.

worked_example.title: Cost the block programme
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a block has 120 schools and 6,000 children. Costs are invented for the exercise.
steps: Readers and kits: 5,000 × 120 = 6,00,000 rupees.
Training for 240 teachers: 2,000 × 240 = 4,80,000 rupees.
Cost per child: 16,44,000 ÷ 6,000 = 274 rupees a year.
worked_example.answer: The total is Rs 16,44,000, about Rs 274 per child per year. Replace the invented prices with local ones.

mistakes: Using a sample survey for individual teachers. Pick the tool from the decision.
Letting the dedicated hour be eaten by exam preparation or census duty.
Scaling without a coach for every 15 to 20 schools.

recall.q: How many steps does the diagnostic card have?
recall.a: Five: aksharas, common words, a Grade 1 paragraph, a Grade 2 story, two questions about the story.

recall.q: How often should the class be reassessed?
recall.a: Every three weeks, with the same card.

recall.q: Which tool answers 'which children in this class need what'?
recall.a: An ASER-style one-on-one card.

recall.q: Name two checklist questions before scaling.
recall.a: Any two of the ten, such as whether the timetable protects daily time or whether there is a coach for every 15 to 20 schools.

recall.q: What target does the example block set?
recall.a: Raise the share reading a Grade 2 story from 30% to 50% in one year.

sections.title: Debates and where next
sections.big_idea: Open debates remain, so a fair report states **the figure, the method, the data year and the language** every time.
in_plain_words: Four debates are unsettled: one speed benchmark for all languages, English medium from Grade 1, technology, and deadlines like 2025. For each, the deck gives the two views and what the evidence says. Akshara learning is slower, hardware alone fails, and ASER 2024 shows real but partial progress.

The reporting table lists six mistakes: comparing ASER with PARAKH, quoting learning poverty without its year, reporting speed alone, calling 70% a measured figure, treating implementation as learning, and ignoring the language of assessment. **Quote the year with every number**: ASER 2026 and later state results will move these figures. The closing page lists related courses.

diagram.note: leave any one out and the number can mislead

key_terms.meaning: Oral reading fluency, usually correct words per minute.
The year of the assessment behind a figure.
A simulated or modelled figure that is no measurement.
A directive, kit or book supplied to schools.
What children can do, measured on children.

worked_example.title: Correct a sentence in a proposal
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a proposal says "Learning poverty in India is 56.1%" with no year.
steps: Find the data year in the table: 2017.
The figure is from 2017, so by 2026 it is 2026 − 2017 = 9 years old.
Add the method: World Bank WDI series SE.LPV.PRIM, resting on a pre-NEP assessment.
Add a caution: pandemic closures probably raised the numbers after 2019.
worked_example.answer: "Learning poverty in India was 56.1% on 2017 data (World Bank WDI), before NEP 2020 and NIPUN Bharat."

mistakes: Quoting a headline figure without its data year, as with India's 2017 learning poverty.
Reading a deadline as a result. Deadlines can focus effort and also encourage inflated reporting.
Reporting kits distributed as learning. Directives and kits are inputs.

recall.q: Which four debates does the table list?
recall.a: One speed benchmark for all languages, English medium from Grade 1, technology for FLN, and deadlines like 2025 or 2026-27.

recall.q: What should you call the 70% learning poverty figure?
recall.a: An estimate, as the World Bank does.

recall.q: What is wrong with reporting words per minute alone?
recall.a: Speed without meaning can be drilled.

recall.q: Which course does the deck suggest for comparing programmes per rupee?
recall.a: Cost Effectiveness 101.

recall.q: What closing advice does the end slide give?
recall.a: Find where each child is, then teach from there.

notes.2: Treat the agenda as a route through the problem. Sections 2 to 4 cover how children learn to read and calculate, section 5 how it is measured, section 6 what policy promises, and sections 7 to 9 evidence and delivery. Section 10 gives you tools to use on Monday.
notes.4: Memorise the two NEP wordings: literacy is the ability to read and comprehend basic text, numeracy is basic addition and subtraction with Indian numerals. NIPUN Bharat splits literacy into five parts a teacher can teach and an assessor can measure. **Foundational is literal**: every later subject builds on it.
notes.5: Keep the phrase "learn to read, then read to learn", with Grade 3 as the turning point. A child who cannot read the Grade 4 chapter falls behind in science as well as reading, and the gap compounds. That is why the early years are the cheap years to fix.
notes.6: A learning profile shows what each grade adds. A shallow one means children move up while learning little. Pritchett and Beatty's surprise is that slowing the curriculum to match children raises learning. Ask of any curriculum whether it moves faster than children can follow. Section 7 shows programmes built on slowing down.
notes.7: Take away three numbers: 2.5 grade levels below standard for the average grade 6 student, 4.5 by grade 9, and a spread of 5 to 6 levels inside one grade. A teacher who teaches to the textbook reaches the top of that range, and the bottom group sits through lessons it cannot follow.
notes.8: Learning poverty is the share of 10-year-olds who cannot read a simple text, with out-of-school children counted as not reading. The 70% and the 78% for South Asia are simulations from school closure data, so call them estimates and predictions. Use them for scale and use measured data for a country.
notes.9: Read each row with its data year. India's 56.1% rests on 2017 data, Bangladesh's 51.2% on 2022, Pakistan's 79.5% on 2019 and Sri Lanka's 14.8% on 2015, and Nepal has no estimate. **Never compare these as if they were one year.** India's figure predates NEP 2020 and NIPUN Bharat.
notes.10: Pritchett's argument is that systems got children into classrooms and neglected learning. RISE took the question to seven countries, including India and Pakistan. For FLN, remember that a mission touches curriculum, teacher training and reward, and measurement. Fixing one part while the others pull the other way rarely holds.
notes.11: Use the course map as the order you meet the problem in the field: how children learn, how we know, what is promised, what works, what you do. Note the labelling rule. Every statistic carries a source and year, and teaching examples marked Illustrative are invented.
notes.13: Learn the five components as a ladder: phonological awareness, phonics, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension. Comprehension is the goal and the other four are the route. The classroom-sign column shows what each looks like in a Hindi-medium Grade 1. A child can be stuck at any single rung, so check them one by one.
notes.14: Before a child can understand a written sentence she has to understand it spoken. Use the practical test: read a short story aloud and ask questions. If she cannot answer when listening, **the problem is language** and more phonics will not fix it. EGRA's listening comprehension subtask measures exactly this.
notes.15: Phonological awareness is about hearing and needs no print. Remember the order of units: syllables, onset and rime, then single phonemes. In akshara scripts the written unit is nearer the syllable, so start with syllable games such as clapping the beats in kamal, and expect phoneme awareness to grow with print.
notes.16: Decoding means working out a word you have never seen. EGRA uses invented words so a child cannot lean on memory. In class, give new combinations of known symbols every day. **Reading the same lesson aloud ten times** trains memory more than decoding.
notes.17: Fluency matters because attention is limited. A child busy working out each akshara has nothing left for the meaning of the sentence. Remember the goals: 45 to 60 words a minute in Grade 2 and at least 60 in Grade 3, always read with meaning. Speed without meaning is a drill.
notes.18: Ask both kinds of question: literal (the answer is in the text) and inferential (the text plus her own reasoning). Then check what your tool measures. ASER's story level has the child read a Std II text but does not test comprehension at that level, so do not report it as reading with understanding.
notes.19: The table is an illustration of a mechanism, built from no study. At 10 words per minute the story takes six minutes and the first line is forgotten. At 60 it takes one minute and is held whole. Set benchmarks per language, because word length and script density differ.
notes.20: Copying from the blackboard looks like writing but tests eye and hand. Dictation shows what a child knows about sounds. Use the task list as a ladder, from writing her own name to one sentence about a story. Portfolios and oral presentations turn written work into evidence of progress.
notes.21: Use the pathway as a diagnostic map. Find the earliest stage where the child is stuck, then start there. The four-row table gives symptom, probable stage and first move. Children work on several stages at once, yet instruction aimed past their stage does not help.
notes.23: Sort scripts into three types. An alphabet's symbol stands for a sound, an abjad's mainly for a consonant, and an alphasyllabary's for a consonant carrying an inherent vowel. Most research is on English, so check what script a finding came from before applying it to Hindi, Tamil or Telugu.
notes.24: Learn the akshara through the table: क is ka, and vowel signs change it. In कि the sign is written before the consonant and read after it. The script is harder to learn than it looks and also largely consistent, so once a child can write an akshara she can usually pronounce it.
notes.25: Nag found akshara knowledge slower to acquire than letter knowledge in English, and phoneme awareness slower to emerge, in low-achieving and effective schools alike. **The pace reflects the script** as well as the teaching. A timeline copied from English research will be too fast, and teachers will be judged to fail.
notes.26: Less fluent readers sat at floor on phoneme tasks while fluent readers showed phonemic awareness, so print knowledge builds it. Begin with syllable awareness and let phoneme awareness follow. Rapid naming also predicts reading rate, which makes a slow namer a child to watch.
notes.27: The akshara in use run into hundreds, and symbol learning continues into middle school, while alphabets are typically complete within a year. Plan to keep teaching symbols through Grade 3. When you argue for script-specific materials, note that NIPUN Bharat's own definitions already use the word akshara.
notes.28: Use the five moves as a design checklist, remembering the slide's caution that no sequence is agreed and the research base is thin. Teach vowel signs as a pattern, start with syllables, add frequent conjuncts early, read connected text from the first weeks. Chanting the barakhadi without reading trains recitation.
notes.29: Plan second scripts by what transfers and what must be learned again. Print standing for speech, phonological awareness and the reading habit transfer. The symbols, the direction of writing for Urdu and English spelling do not. NEP para 4.12 puts early reading in the mother tongue and other languages from Grade 3.
notes.31: NIPUN Bharat's numeracy list starts before counting and runs to shapes, measurement, data and patterns. Use the six rows as a checklist for any numeracy programme. One that teaches only sums leaves most of foundational numeracy out.
notes.32: Number sense means knowing that the last number counted is the total, that 8 is more than 5, and that numbers sit in order. Siegler and Ramani found low-income preschoolers behind before school, partly from less informal number play. A child without it learns sums as symbol drills.
notes.33: In four 15-minute sessions, a numbered linear board game closed the gap in numerical estimation, and the same game with colours did nothing. The study was in the United States with small samples. Treat it as a cheap idea to test in anganwadis, such as a numbered snakes and ladders track.
notes.34: Place value is where many children stall. ASER 2024 shows 33.7% of Std III children can subtract with borrowing and 45.8% of Std VIII children can divide. Teach tens with bundles first, trade ten ones for one ten with your hands, and write the borrowing procedure last.
notes.35: Children who calculate at work could not solve equal abstract problems, and school children did better on simple abstract problems but only 1% answered an applied market problem. Neither group transfers its skills. Start from money, measures and trade, and connect them explicitly to written numbers.
notes.36: Follow the five steps of the subtraction lesson: concrete, pictorial, symbolic, talk, apply. Each step links to the one before so the symbol keeps its meaning. The routine is an illustration. Remember that a numeracy lesson is also a language lesson, since word problems need reading.
notes.37: Read the lakshya as a checklist for a diagnostic: numerals to 10 in Balvatika, to 99 in Grade 1, to 999 in Grade 2, to 9999 in Grade 3. The Ministry has since moved the end point to Grade 2. Compare ASER 2024: only a third of Std III children can do the subtraction expected by Grade 2.
notes.39: A written test is a reading test for a child who cannot read, so it records zero without saying where she is stuck. A ladder of skills, tested one child at a time, shows where to start. The cost is people and time, about a day for a class of 40.
notes.40: Know ASER's design: a household survey, children tested at home so out-of-school children count, the same method since 2006. Learn the two ladders: letters, words, Std I paragraph, Std II story; then numbers 1 to 9, 11 to 99, subtraction, division. A child is marked at her highest comfortable level.
notes.41: Reading in government schools in 2024 is the highest for Std III since the survey began, which is real progress. Keep the level in view: more than three in four government school Std III children could not read a Std II text, and 27.1% of all rural Std III children could.
notes.42: Read the table across 2018, 2022 and 2024. Std III subtraction in all schools went 28.2%, 25.9%, 33.7%, a dip then a gain. The Std VIII line barely moves, from 44.1% to 45.8%, which is the case for remedial work in upper primary.
notes.43: Foundational learning starts before school. Anganwadi centres are the largest provider for ages 3 and 4, and enrolment has risen since 2018. Enrolment only shows a child is registered, so ask what happens inside the centre. The share of underage children in Std I fell to 16.7%.
notes.44: The headline hides the spread. Std III children occupy every level of the reading ladder, and nearly a third could not yet read words. A lesson pitched at the Std III textbook reaches only the top group, which is the whole case for grouping children by level.
notes.45: State figures differ by a factor of seven: Himachal Pradesh 49.7% against Telangana 6.8% in 2024. Uttar Pradesh more than doubled its 2018 level, while Telangana barely moved after the pandemic fall. Do not explain gaps with one cause. Ask how each state's programme was delivered.
notes.46: FLS 2022 tested over 86,000 Grade 3 children one-on-one in 20 languages. In numeracy 42% met global minimum proficiency, a further 10% exceeded it, and 11% could not do the most basic tasks. Each language sample is also a state system, so compare languages with care.
notes.47: PARAKH tests children in school on written items and reports an average score. ASER tests at home on a floor-level ladder and reports the share reaching a level. A 64% average and a 23% reading rate (ASER, government school Std III) can both be true. **Quote each with its method.**
notes.48: EGRA and EGMA are oral, one-on-one toolkits with the core subtasks in the table. Remember the Toolkit's warning: EGRA is not meant for high-stakes decisions on promotion or on individual teachers. Using it that way invites teaching to the test.
notes.50: Remember two paragraphs. Para 2.1 estimates over 5 crore children had not attained FLN, and para 2.2 makes universal FLN in primary school by 2025 the highest priority, with the rest of the Policy relevant only once this is achieved. The list shows the supporting actions.
notes.51: Learn the structure as ages: foundational 3 to 8, preparatory 8 to 11, middle 11 to 14, secondary 14 to 18. The foundational stage joins three years of pre-school to Grades 1 and 2. The policy has no statutory force, and early childhood care rests on Article 45, a directive principle.
notes.52: NIPUN Bharat launched on 5 July 2021 under Samagra Shiksha. Its target year moved from the policy's 2025 to 2026-27, and Ministry replies since December 2025 describe the goal as the end of Grade 2, with no year stated. Always check which version of the goal a document is quoting.
notes.53: The literacy goals use an unknown text, which rules out reciting the class reader, and attach meaning to speed. Note the caution: one national words-per-minute figure across 20-plus languages sits uneasily with Nag's evidence and with FLS 2022, which set benchmarks per language.
notes.54: Vidya Pravesh is a 12-week, four-hours-a-day module at the start of Grade 1. It reached 1,80,13,930 students in 2022-23. Keep the slide's warning in mind: a school reporting that a programme ran is a different thing from children being ready. Check what was done in the room.
notes.55: Keep the framework and the kit apart. NCF-FS sets goals and pedagogy for ages 3 to 8, and states write curricula from it in their own languages. Jadui Pitara is the play-based kit. A kit is only as good as the routine around it, so ask which materials reached which classrooms.
notes.56: Use the table as a legal toolkit. Section 29(2)(e) backs activity-based teaching, 29(2)(f) mother tongue, 29(2)(h) continuous evaluation, and 24(1)(d) a duty to assess and supplement instruction. The proviso to section 4 covers late entrants. Cite the section when you argue for a practice.
notes.57: Section 16 was rewritten in 2019. Classes 5 and 8 now have a regular exam, and a child who fails gets additional instruction and a re-examination within two months. Holding back does nothing for reading. **Remediation earlier is cheaper** than detention later.
notes.58: Take stock as of October 2026. The 2025 target has passed and 2026-27 is the current year. ASER 2024 shows real gains, largest in government schools, yet 27.1% of rural Std III children read a Std II text. Quote the year with every figure.
notes.60: Memorise the Great Buys: information on benefits and costs, structured pedagogy, and targeting instruction by learning level. Bad Buys are inputs alone, such as laptops or textbooks when other problems stay unaddressed. The slide discloses that panel members' own programmes are among those rated.
notes.61: TaRL has five steps: assess, group, teach, reassess, return. Children are grouped by what they can do, across grades if needed, for a fixed part of the day, and they move up as soon as they are ready. J-PAL counts six randomised evaluations in seven Indian states.
notes.62: The balsakhi study found a 0.28 SD gain, largest for the weakest children, and 0.47 SD in maths from computer-assisted learning. About 0.10 SD remained a year after. Two lessons: teaching weaker children at their level works even with lightly trained tutors, and gains fade unless the classroom builds on them.
notes.63: Compare the three Jaunpur arms. Information and testing tools changed nothing, while reading camps raised reading sharply: a non-reader who attended was 60 points more likely to decipher letters. Giving communities information did not change schools. **Give them a specific task** instead.
notes.64: Read the table for the failure and the successes. Teachers in Bihar and Uttarakhand did not adopt TaRL, Haryana gained 0.15 SD in language, and Uttar Pradesh camps gained 0.61 to 0.70 SD. A method needs protected time, mentoring and a mandate to survive a regular timetable.
notes.65: Mindspark tests each child and serves content at her actual level, often several grades below her class. Lottery winners gained 0.37 SD in maths and 0.23 SD in Hindi after 4.5 months. Gains were similar for all, so relative gains were largest for the weakest. GEEAP rates it promising, with limited evidence.
notes.66: Structured pedagogy is a package of lesson plans, materials and ongoing support, and any part alone is weaker. The Nepal case shows scale: USD 71 million over five years across all 77 districts. Learn the failure modes: rigid scripts, late books, and coaching that turns into inspection.
notes.67: Use the table with its years. Pakistan 79.5% (2019), Bangladesh 51.2% (2022), Sri Lanka 14.8% (2015). ASER Pakistan 2025 found 51% of Class 5 children reading a Class 2 text. Compare data years before drawing conclusions across countries.
notes.68: Inputs are needed, and alone they fail. The input trap is a district buying graded readers that stay in a cupboard. Tie each input to a routine, a trained teacher and a check on whether children read the books. Counting books actually used, 51.3% of government schools, is the right measure.
notes.70: Quote NEP para 4.11 with its qualifier: wherever possible, the medium of instruction until at least Grade 5 is the home language. Where materials do not exist, teachers should still talk in the home language and use bilingual materials. Remember a child can decode a language she does not understand.
notes.71: Rank the sources by force. Article 350A is an obligation of endeavour, RTE s 29(2)(f) says "as far as practicable", NEP is policy and cannot be enforced in court, and the 2014 Constitution Bench judgment binds. Know which one you are citing before you design a programme in a minority language.
notes.72: The 2014 judgment held that parents choose the medium, protected by Article 19(1)(a) and, for private and minority schools, Articles 19(1)(g), 29 and 30. Government schools can be asked to teach in the mother tongue. Private unaided schools cannot be compelled, and parental demand for English is a fact.
notes.73: A room with four or five home languages cannot have mother tongue instruction for each. Use the six moves: let children answer in any language, build two-language word lists, use bilingual books, recruit local assistants, teach the school language orally first, and include sign language.
notes.74: MTB-MLE starts in the mother tongue, then adds the state language, then English. Makwana's review reports it in Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand and finds better early literacy and engagement. The evidence is mostly government reports, so build an evaluation into any new programme.
notes.75: Separate the three sources of a language gap: script complexity, mismatch between home and school language, and the quality of teaching. A listening comprehension check splits decoding from language. Always state the language of assessment, since a Grade 3 result in English, Hindi and Tamil measures three things.
notes.76: Use the decision table as a starting point and test it locally. Match the first reading language to the home language situation, then add the bridge: oral English early, standard vocabulary, a bridge by Grade 3, local assistants. For private schools the choice rests with the school and parents.
notes.78: NIPUN Bharat relies on the existing teachers, trained mainly through NISHTHA. Think of teacher need as knowledge and practice: how reading and number develop, then daily routines. Training should make the RTE duty under s 24(1)(d) doable, which is to assess each child and supplement instruction.
notes.79: A meta-analysis of 60 studies found coaching raised instructional practice by 0.49 SD and student achievement by 0.18 SD, mostly in the United States. Larger trials show smaller effects. A coach with 15 schools can visit often; one with 60 schools and administrative duties becomes an inspector.
notes.80: Use the slide's checklist for any training design: is it subject-specific, do teachers practise in the session, who visits the classroom afterwards? Programmes with larger gains link participation to career incentives and include lesson enactment. Government programmes at scale usually lack these features.
notes.81: In 2024, 52.1% of government primary schools had fewer than 60 students, and two-thirds of Std I and II classrooms were multigrade. The RTE Schedule allows two teachers for up to 60 children, so a small school is by law a multigrade school. Choose materials that come in a multigrade version.
notes.82: Children learn to read by reading many easy texts in a language they know. Graded readers start with only the aksharas taught so far. Libraries alone do not work, but a daily reading period does. Books other than textbooks were used in 51.3% of government primary schools in 2024.
notes.83: Check time on task with the table: teacher attendance 87.5%, student attendance 75.9%, and the RTE rules on staffing and duties. Section 27 allows teachers to be deployed only for the census, disaster relief and elections. The Census reference date of 1 March 2027 is a calendar risk.
notes.84: A randomised trial gave mothers literacy classes, training in helping children, or both. All three had significant but modest effects on children's maths, and mothers' own scores rose. Family programmes work best beside classroom change. Phones are a channel, though GEEAP rates mobile learning as promising only.
notes.85: Communities do best with specific tasks that have a clear product, such as a reading camp or ten minutes of listening to a child read. Information alone did nothing in Jaunpur. For child-wise apps, DPDP s 9 consent and the ban on tracking apply from 13 May 2027, so design to that standard now.
notes.87: Make one card in the school language and test children one at a time. Steps 1 to 4 follow the ASER ladder, and step 5 adds comprehension and application. Mark the highest level each child reaches comfortably. Repeat at the start, middle and end of the year on one class sheet.
notes.88: Check the illustrative class: five reading levels hold 4, 9, 9, 8 and 10 children, 40 in all, grouped into A to D. The teacher works with Group A, peers help, and reassessment every three weeks moves children up. The aim is that Group A is empty by term end.
notes.89: Start from the decision, then pick the tool. An ASER-style card tells a teacher which children need what. An adapted EGRA or EGMA with a comparison group tests a programme. PARAKH suits state progress. **Never use a sample survey** to judge an individual teacher or school.
notes.90: Read each row as situation, strongest option, evidence. Children far below grade level: level-based grouping. Willing teachers unsure how to teach reading: structured pedagogy. No protected time: volunteer camps. Treat the table as a start for a theory of change, then test it.
notes.91: Follow the five-step plan for the block: diagnose, design, support, materials, review. The target of 30% to 50% sits against two benchmarks: 0.61 to 0.70 SD from intensive camps is an upper bound, and 0.15 SD is a sober figure for a teacher-led hour. Plan for census duty and late materials.
notes.92: Check the cost arithmetic: every component is priced, the total is divided by children reached, and the indicators are named in advance. Replace the invented figures with local prices. The structure is the lesson: cost every component, divide by children reached, and decide what you will check.
notes.93: Run the ten questions before expanding a pilot. They come from TaRL, where a volunteer method failed with government teachers, and from coaching, where effects shrink at scale. A yes to all ten does not guarantee success, but any no is a known reason for failure.
notes.95: Treat each row as an open question. One speed benchmark? Akshara learning is slower. English medium from Grade 1? Parents choose in private schools. Technology? Mindspark worked, and hardware alone is a Bad Buy. Deadlines? Progress is real but partial. Say which view your evidence supports.
notes.96: Use the table when you write or review a report. Each row pairs a mistake with its correction: name the method, the year and the language. Call 70% learning poverty an estimate. Report fluency with comprehension. Count outcomes measured on children, and treat directives and kits as inputs.
notes.97: Use the ten points as revision. If you keep two things, keep Grade 3 as the turning point and the figure that about one in four rural Std III children reads a Std II text. Each figure is sourced where it first appeared, and ASER 2026 may move them.
notes.98: Use the glossary to fix the acronyms: FLN, ORF, ASER, FLS, PARAKH, EGRA and EGMA, NIPUN Bharat, Vidya Pravesh, TaRL. Note two dates, PARAKH on 8 February 2023 and NIPUN Bharat on 5 July 2021, and that NIPUN Bharat's end point has moved from Grade 3 to Grade 2.
notes.99: Pick your next course by the thread you need. Education Policy 101 for systems, Child Development 101 for the early years, Impact Evaluation 101 for evidence, Item Response Theory 101 for how test forms share a scale, and Cost Effectiveness 101 for comparing programmes per rupee.
